title: Climate Resilience Initiative in Malawi -CRIM  Phase-11
description: CRIM-II aims at bridging the existing gap of market opportunities for entrepreneurs, expanding production activities that bring alternative sources of livelihoods, and improving and integrating watershed management/ecosystem-based management approaches and climate change adaptation planning. The project will support in sustaining development gains made by the communities to date, including scaling viable entrepreneurship opportunities, proven under CRIM-I and prospecting new investments within the scope of climate change, adaptation and resilience building. The Private Sector shall become the enabler for adaptation and resilience-building.Ultimately, CRIM-II is expected to ultimately result into improved market opportunities for climate entrepreneurs; increased sources of livelihoods through expansion of production activities; improved and integrating watershed management/ecosystem-based management and improved climate change adaptation planning. This will be achieved through implementation of interrelated activities aimed to ensure:a)	Strengthening integrated watershed protection.b)	Strengthening the adaptive capacity of vulnerable households and reducing exposure to climate risks.c)	Enhancing private sector engagement and climate entrepreneurship

title: The Biodiversity Finance Initiative – Phase II (BIOFIN Malawi)
description: The Biodiversity Finance Initiative – BIOFIN – is a global programme that developed, piloted, and is continuously improving a methodology to measure existing biodiversity expenditure levels, assess future financial needs, and design comprehensive plans to use finance tools and solutions that increase financing, effectiveness and efficiency of biodiversity management in 30 countries. BIOFIN’s first phase (2012-2018) enabled full assessments and initial implementation of finance plan elements in target countries. Significant scaling up of finance solutions is required in all countries to address the biodiversity finance challenge. BIOFIN’s second phase enables the 30 countries to complete the design and implementation of priority finance solutions and will allow a further 15 countries to undertake the assessments and create the finance plan. At the central level, knowledge management platforms will be expanded and additional guidance produced for most valuable finance solutions.

title: Second National Climate Resilience Project (NCRP2)
description: In support of the Government of Malawi’s (GoM) ongoing adaptation and resilience building efforts, UNDP and the Environmental Affairs Department (EAD) have collaborated on the development of the Second National Climate Resilience Project ‘NCRP2’ — a policy-level project aimed at continuing the legacy of the original ‘NCRP1’. NCRP2 addresses a significant development challenge in Malawi, namely the limited systemic impact of resilience-building efforts in climate change (CC) and environmental and natural resource management (ENRM). Despite Malawi’s robust policy environment for CC and ENRM, systemic impact from the operationalisation of these policies has been slow, complicating the country’s goal of sustainable, climate-resilient economic growth as described in Malawi 2063 Vision, the country’s overarching development agenda. title: Advancing Energy Access and Sustainability PIP
description: The Access to Clean and Renewable Energy (ACRE) project is being implemented by the Ministry of Energy in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme. The Project commenced in 2020 and was expected to conclude in 2023, but it was granted an extension and will conclude in November 2024.The primary objective of UNDP energy programming is to increase access to modern electricity services in isolated rural communities through commercially viable mini-grids with a focus on the productive use of energy that operates in a self-sustaining manner and promotion of clean energy transition through innovative financing mechanisms for homes and industries, catalysing sustainable solar for health facilities and institutional capacity strengthening. The Advancing Energy Access and Sustainability Project Initiation Plan was developed as a bridging tool as the project design to succeed the Access to Clean and Renewable Energy project is finalised. The key objective of the initiation plan is to extend mini-grid distribution networks in selected sites, conduct an assessment to better understand UNDPs niche in providing energy solutions within the context of Malawis energy situation and strengthen the institutional structures and governance capacities for better mini-grid operations.

title: Catalyze Malawi: Sustainable Green Transition, Entrepreneurship Growth, and Alternative Finance Project
description: Malawi faces significant structural and economic challenges, rooted in its reliance on an undiversified, agro-based economy that accounts for approximately 30% of GDP and 80% of export earnings. This over-reliance exposes the country to vulnerabilities such as climate shocks, environmental degradation, and macroeconomic instability. Key barriers include limited investment in transformative sectors like trade, energy, and digital technology, compounded by logistical challenges due to its landlocked geography, high transportation costs, and inadequate infrastructure.A cascade of shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical tensions, and local economic instability, has further undermined the country’s development gains and business environment.The Catalyze Malawi: Sustainable Green Transition, Entrepreneurship Growth, and Alternative Finance Project(2025–2028) aims to contribute in addressing such pressing issues by fostering sustainable economic growth andresilience through:1.	Alternative Financing Mechanisms: Unlocking innovative financial solutions, such as green and blue bonds, to fund sustainable business growth and mobilize investments in Malawi’s green transition.2.	Improved Business Environment: Strengthening the regulatory and operational framework to foster inclusive and green economic growth, reduce barriers to investment, and enable private sector competitiveness.3.	Entrepreneurial Growth: Advancing startups and SMEs from idea stage to growth-oriented, export-ready enterprises, with an emphasis on women- and youth-led businesses.4.	Green Transition: Supporting Malawi’s shift to a sustainable economy through investments in green businesses, clean energy solutions, and environmentally friendly practices.5.	Agricultural Commercialization: Transitioning the agricultural sector into a commercially viable and market-oriented system, increasing productivity and value addition.By 2028, the project envisions a more resilient Malawian economy

title: UCHI - Ulimi ndi Chilengedwe m’Malawi: Strengthening Agricultural Commercialisation
description: Agriculture is the backbone of Malawis economy, employing over 70% of the population and contributing significantly to the countrys Gross Domestic Product (GDP) (24.7%). Whilst subsistence farming has been the predominant practice, there has been a growing emphasis on commercialization to unlock the sectors full potential. Commercialization entails transitioning from traditional, subsistence-oriented farming to more market-oriented, profit-driven agricultural activities in line with the Government’s Agriculture, Tourism and Mining (ATM) growth strategy. The overall development challenge that the UCHI project seeks to address is the low productivity and commercialization of agriculture in Malawi, which significantly hampers economic growth and exacerbates poverty, particularly among smallholder farmers.

title: Risk Informed Development for Resilience (RID4R)
description: The Risk-Informed Development for Resilience (RID4R) project, implemented by DoDMA with support from UNDP, aims to strengthen Malawi’s resilience to climate-related and other hazards through risk-informed development planning and systems enhancement. The project is aligned with the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, the Malawi 2063 vision, the National Resilience Strategy (NRS), and the 2023 Disaster Risk Management Act.RID4R adopts a systems approach to resilience by enhancing anticipatory, absorptive, adaptive, and transformative capacities at national, district, and community levels. Specifically, the project seeks to:Strengthen disaster response and preparedness systems for multi-hazard scenarios, building anticipatory capacities.Promote risk-informed planning, financing, and accountability frameworks that address the underlying drivers of vulnerability.The project targets vulnerable communities within five local authorities—Nkhotakota, Salima, Dedza, Zomba City, and Mzuzu City—which have experienced significant impacts from disasters, including Cyclone Freddy in 2023 and El Niño-induced dry spells in 2024. These districts have recorded substantial losses in productive sectors, public infrastructure, and basic services. For instance, Cyclone Freddy caused widespread destruction of homes, schools, health facilities, and roads, while Lake Malawi backflows in Salima and Nkhotakota disrupted livelihoods and access to critical services.Drawing on lessons from the previous DRM4R initiative, RID4R emphasizes inclusive implementation, community engagement, institutional capacity strengthening, and the creation of knowledge systems for informed decision-making.
